moderate.bluf: Transitioning economies offering higher growth with greater risks.

expert.bluf: Incomplete capital account liberalization; procyclical flows, dollar sensitivity.

beginner.bluf: When investors rapidly move money out of a country.

moderate.bluf: Large outflows from instability or confidence loss.

expert.bluf: Measurable via BOP capital account, banking foreign assets, errors & omissions.

beginner.bluf: Foreign Direct Investment - when a company or investor from one country builds a factory, buys a business, or makes a lasting investment in another country.

moderate.bluf: Long-term cross-border investment involving control or significant influence (typically >10% equity stake). More stable than portfolio flows. Reflects structural competitiveness and business environment.

expert.bluf: BPM6 definition: >10% equity stake conferring managerial influence. FDI-financed current account deficits are structurally stable vs portfolio-flow-financed deficits. Greenfield vs M&A distinction matters for real economic impact. China+1 diversification reshaping global FDI patterns.

beginner.bluf: Foreign Portfolio Investment - when foreign investors buy stocks and bonds in another country without controlling the companies.

moderate.bluf: Cross-border investment in financial assets (equities, bonds) without management control (<10% stake). More volatile than FDI - can reverse quickly in risk-off environments.

expert.bluf: Short-duration, return-seeking capital flows. FPI sensitivity to rate differentials and risk appetite makes it procyclical and potentially destabilising. EM FPI flows tracked via IIF data; sudden reversals are the canonical 'sudden stop' trigger.

beginner.bluf: When a country has both a government budget deficit and a trade deficit at the same time - they often go hand in hand.

moderate.bluf: The theory that fiscal deficits cause current account deficits via the national accounting identity: CA = (S − I) + (T − G). When government dissaving (T − G < 0) isn't offset by private saving, the external balance deteriorates.

expert.bluf: Hypothesis linking fiscal and external deficits through the S-I = CA + (G-T) identity. Empirically conditional: holds in economies near full employment with flexible FX (Chinn 2005), weakened by Ricardian offset. The US is the canonical example; Reagan-era and current fiscal expansions both associated with CA deterioration.

beginner.bluf: Money moving between countries - investors buying foreign stocks, companies building factories abroad, or banks lending across borders.

moderate.bluf: Cross-border movement of money for investment: FDI (long-term, stable), portfolio flows (equities/bonds, volatile), and banking flows (loans/deposits). Direction and composition determine a country's external vulnerability.

expert.bluf: Decompose into FDI, portfolio, other (banking), and reserve flows. Rey (2013) argues a 'global financial cycle' driven by US monetary policy governs capital flow dynamics, reducing the trilemma to a dilemma. Sudden stops (Calvo 1998) occur when gross inflows reverse - EM vulnerability depends on the composition and currency denomination of liabilities.

beginner.bluf: Taking a position to protect against potential losses. Like buying insurance for your investments.

moderate.bluf: Risk management technique: taking offsetting positions to reduce exposure to adverse price movements. Currency hedging (FX forwards), interest rate hedging (swaps), and equity hedging (put options) are common examples.

expert.bluf: Offset of unwanted risk exposures via derivatives or cash positions. Perfect hedge eliminates risk but also upside. Cross-hedging (using correlated but different instruments) introduces basis risk. Dynamic hedging (delta/gamma) creates mechanical market impact - short gamma positions require buying highs and selling lows, amplifying volatility.

beginner.bluf: The current account measures whether a country earns more from the rest of the world than it spends. It tracks trade in goods and services, plus income flows like investment returns and remittances.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: A current account deficit means a country is spending more abroad than it earns - it needs foreign money to fill the gap. This makes it dependent on foreign investors being willing to lend. A surplus means the country is a net saver, lending money to the rest of the world.

sections.head: Intuition
sections.body: Imagine your household's relationship with the outside world. You earn money (exports, investment income) and you spend money (imports, money sent abroad). If you spend more than you earn, you borrow the difference from abroad. The current account is this balance for an entire country.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: A current account of -3% of GDP means the country spent 3% more on foreign goods, services, and transfers than it earned. The US runs a persistent deficit (it imports more than it exports). Germany and Japan run surpluses (they export more than they import). China's surplus means it accumulates foreign reserves.

sections.head: What to watch
body: Deficits beyond -4% of GDP make a currency vulnerable - they need constant foreign financing
Surpluses above +5% invite trade tensions and accusations of currency manipulation
Oil price swings dramatically affect current accounts of energy importers and exporters
The current account must always mirror the financial account - deficits are funded by capital inflows

beginner.formal: The sum of a country's trade balance (goods and services), net primary income (investment returns), and net secondary income (transfers and remittances), expressed as a percentage of GDP.

moderate.bluf: The current account balance reflects a country's net external position - the sum of trade, income, and transfer flows. Persistent deficits require capital account financing and create FX vulnerability; surpluses accumulate net foreign assets.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: The current account is the external constraint. A deficit country needs foreign capital inflows to finance the gap - if those flows reverse, the currency collapses (classic balance of payments crisis). For markets, widening deficits put pressure on the exchange rate and increase sovereign risk. The twin deficits hypothesis links fiscal and current account deficits through national savings.

sections.head: Intuition
sections.body: The current account identity: CA = S - I (savings minus investment). A deficit means the country invests more than it saves - not necessarily bad if the investment is productive. The US deficit reflects both high investment and low savings. Germany's surplus reflects high savings and weak domestic investment - a different problem.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: The UK ran a current account deficit of ~4% of GDP in 2022. When the Truss mini-budget spooked markets, foreign investors briefly questioned whether they wanted to keep financing that deficit. Sterling fell 10% in days. This is the current account vulnerability channel in action - deficits are fine until the capital flows that finance them aren't.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Financing composition:** FDI-financed deficits are stable; portfolio-flow-financed deficits are fragile
**NIIP:** net international investment position - cumulative current account balance over time
**Terms of trade:** commodity price shifts can swing the current account 2-3% of GDP for resource economies
**Real exchange rate:** persistent overvaluation worsens the current account - the correction is usually sharp

moderate.formal: The current account balance as a percentage of GDP. Composed of: trade balance + net primary income (investment returns) + net secondary income (transfers). By accounting identity: current account + capital account + financial account = 0.

expert.bluf: The current account is the mirror image of the financial account. The savings-investment balance (S-I = CA) determines external financing needs. For EM, the current account is the binding constraint; for DM with reserve currencies, the constraint is softer but not absent, as GBP in 2022 demonstrated.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: The current account determines the rate of change of the net international investment position (NIIP). The US NIIP is -$20tn (~-70% of GDP) - the world's largest debtor position - yet it earns positive net investment income because US foreign assets earn higher returns than US liabilities pay (the exorbitant privilege). This privilege persists only as long as dollar reserve status holds.

sections.head: Intuition
sections.body: The intertemporal current account approach: today's deficit is a claim on future surpluses. If the deficit finances productive investment, it is self-correcting. If it finances consumption (the US pattern), it requires either future fiscal adjustment or perpetual willingness of foreigners to hold your debt. The Feldstein-Horioka puzzle showed savings and investment are more correlated within countries than theory predicts - capital is less mobile than assumed.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: Japan's persistent current account surplus (~3-4% of GDP) finances its own government debt domestically - a key reason JGB yields stayed low despite 250% debt-to-GDP. Contrast with Turkey: persistent CA deficits (~-5%) financed by hot money meant that any loss of confidence triggered a currency crisis (lira lost 80%+ from 2018-2023).

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Basic balance:** current account + net FDI - the stable financing component. If negative, the country relies on flighty portfolio flows
**Valuation effects:** NIIP changes from asset price movements can dwarf the current account flow
**Reserve adequacy:** Guidotti rule - reserves should cover 12 months of short-term external debt. Below this, crisis risk rises sharply
**Global imbalances:** large surplus countries (China, Germany) are exporting demand deficiency - trade tensions are the political manifestation

expert.formal: The current account balance as % of GDP. Identity: CA = S - I = -(KA + FA). The intertemporal budget constraint requires the present value of future current accounts to sum to the initial NIIP - deficits today must be offset by surpluses eventually.
